newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK --All eyes on nonfarm payrolls.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK --All eyes on nonfarm payrolls.

text.p: Heavy trading of U.S. government securities was expected Friday as players nervously awaited December's nonfarm payrolls report.
The report was to be released by the Labor Department at 830 EST/1330 GMT.

A group of economists surveyed by Reuters expected, on average, that the report would show that 192,000 new jobs were created in December versus 118,000 in November and that the rate of unemployment dipped to 5.3 percent from 5.4 percent the prior month.
Two components of the report also will be scrutinized -- average hourly earnings and manufacturing payrolls.

Economists polled by Reuters expected hourly earnings would rise 0.2 percent, lower than November's 0.8 percent. Meanwhile, most private economists expect factory payrolls to rise by 10,000. But in light of last week's strong National Association of Purchasing Management's survey, a stronger number of new factory jobs could panic the bond market.
Thanksgiving also occurred a week later than usual -- a factor that may inflate the December numbers -- but most analysts have already warned their traders of this.

"I think the market's been fearing a stronger report in the last few days, so if we see anything below 150,000 (new jobs) it will be viewed as very bullish," said Kathy Bostjancic, money market analyst at UBS Securities Inc.
She expected a tepid reaction should the numbers come in close to consensus, but added that anything wildly different than consensus expectations could cause sharp movements.

UBS's expectations were in line with most, calling for about a 190,000 gain in jobs during the month with factory payrolls rising 10,000; the unemployment rate dipping to 5.3 percent and workweek hours remaining steady at 34.5.
A rally Thursday was prompted as investors covered positions they feared might be too short the market, said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial analyst at First National Bank of Chicago.
"Many people will just be sitting on the fence ahead of the payrolls report Friday," Karydakis said. "On balance, the PPI number was viewed as being favorable."
Karydakis said the 6.75 percent bond yield area was suddenly appearing to have value to investors and the reality of a 6.80 percent level wasn't seen as that bad either.
"The issue will be resolved Friday," he said.

The Fed's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee next meets on February 4 and 5, and many analysts believe the majority of policymakers were looking to December's payrolls data as one of the first major piece of evidence needed to assess just how strong the U.S. economy grew in the fourth quarter of last year.

A stronger-than-anticipated payrolls report coupled with a strong NAPM report would be bearish for bonds. Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has said in the past that he regards NAPM as a leading rather than lagging indication on where the economy is going -- leading to market fears of a tighening in February.
In late trading Thursday the 30-year bond was up 1-2/32 at 96-23/32 to yield 6.76 percent.

The two-year note was at 99-21/32 to yield 5.94 percent, up 4/32. The five-year note was up 12/32 at 99-14/32 to yield 6.26 percent, while the 10-year note was at 100-00/32, up 21/32, to yield 6.50 percent.
Federal funds closed at 5.25 percent, right at the Federal Reserve's current target level and were expected to open trade Friday at 5-3/16 percent.
